CZ Gate Chip Views

Six-mode CZ gate: tentative chip and EM views

Circuit, floorplan and coupler-level electromagnetic views for the MZI-based post-selected CZ gate, built to show chip-level work now and to prepare the COMSOL validation that is planned.

Tentative. The EM panels come from a finite-difference mode solver written for this project (quasi-TE, semi-vectorial; Si 220 nm core, SiO₂ cladding, 1550 nm). They are pre-COMSOL estimates, not COMSOL results. Layout dimensions marked “assumed” are typical values to confirm with a foundry design kit.
Validation status. Cross-checked against an independent full-vector solver (femwell): coupling strength within about 4%, gap sensitivity within 1%. Width sensitivity differs by about 18%, and the finite-difference solver’s absolute effective index is about 2% high. COMSOL validation is planned and has not been done.
New here? What each tab shows
  • Circuit: the gate as three interferometers on six waveguides, and the paths the two photons take.
  • Gate results: every figure of the project with what to say about it.
  • Chip layout (to scale): the exact reference layout (also a GDS file), coupler and cross-section views for COMSOL, and the thermal model re-run on it.
  • EM model: how strongly two neighbouring waveguides couple, and how that changes with gap, width and wavelength.
  • Fabrication to fidelity: nanometre errors turned into gate fidelity, and what heater retuning recovers.
  • Additions: extra studies that prepare for COMSOL (photon indistinguishability, heater crosstalk, the solver cross-check).
  • Bends & thermal: the extra coupling in the curved sections, and heat leaking between heaters.
  • Phase shifters: heaters versus electro-optic shifters, and what each does to F and P.

Everything here is a software model with assumed geometry where marked. None of it is measured data.

Labels on every panel: Computed Assumed geometry Literature values To scale Schematic, not to scale Illustrative only

Circuit: three MZIs on six modes

In plain words: Three small interferometers (MZIs) each act on a pair of the six waveguides. The gate flips the sign of the |11⟩ state only. It counts as successful only when one photon is found in each logical pair, which happens 1 time in 9.

Each MZI is two 50:50 directional couplers with a heater-controlled phase between them. The three MZIs act on mode pairs (m0,m1), (m2,m3) and (m4,m5). The logical qubits sit on m1–m2 and m3–m4, so m0 and m5 are vacuum ancilla modes. Choose an input state to light up the two photon paths.

Schematic, not to scale · topology, mode order and heater positions exact; lengths not to scale Computed · amplitudes from gate_core.py

Selected input Computed · gate_core.py

Nominal MZI settings (from gate_core.py BASE)

MZIModesαβHeaters
Am0, m1−70.53°0°φ₁, φ₂, θ₁
Bm2, m3+70.53°180°φ₁, φ₂, θ₁
Cm4, m5+70.53°180°φ₁, φ₂, θ₁

α = 2·asin(1/√3) sets the effective 1/3 splitting. The model has 6 phase parameters (α and β per MZI), of which 5 matter: β_A only shifts the empty mode m0. The chip has 9 physical heaters. Ideal gate: F = 1, P = 1/9. These are the code's settings, which use real 50:50 couplers; the paper's Eq. 20 writes the same gate with an idealised MZI matrix (+α for A, β_B = 0). Both conventions give F = 1 and P = 1/9.

Chip layout, to scale To scaleComputed · 14_reference_layout.py

Shows: The exact reference layout (the same polygons as the GDS file): three MZIs, nine heaters with two wires each, 18 pads, test cells.

What to say: Every dimension comes from the simulations or is a stated assumption kept identical to the thermal model. The thermal model was re-run on exactly this layout.

Hessian against the exact model Computed · gate_sim_full.py

Shows: Mean F with random phase errors on the six MZI coordinates α, β: exact six-mode Monte Carlo (dots) against the Hessian formula, paper Eq. 35 (line).

What to say: The quadratic formula is reliable up to about 6° of phase noise; the largest gap is about 0.005 at 8°. For single physical heaters the centre value is 4.5 instead of 4.25 (errata E6).

Phase-control budget Computed · 12_fig5_fig6.py

Shows: Allowed rms phase error for mean F ≥ 0.99: the same for every phase (3.4°), or shared by the Hessian (α_B 1.76°, β 5.1°, α_A and α_C 7.2°).

What to say: α_B needs about four times tighter control than α_A and α_C. That is a design rule for heater drivers.

Coupler errors and recalibration Computed · gate_sim_full.py

Shows: Six couplers with random T = 0.5 ± ε, 100 chips per point: mean F and the fraction of chips with F ≥ 0.999, for no tuning, tuning α only (paper) and tuning all phases.

What to say: Tuning only α barely helps because the error is mostly a phase; tuning all phases restores F = 1 for every chip tested.

Recalibration reach Computed · gate_sim_full.py

Shows: Same error on all couplers: best F after recalibration against ε, with the derived limit |ε| ≤ 1/(2√3) = 0.289.

What to say: Beyond 0.289 an MZI cannot reach the 2/3 splitting any more, so no phase setting recovers the gate. In gap terms that is −38 to +58 nm.

Cascades Computed · gate_sim_full.py

Shows: Cluster-state chains up to 8 qubits built from the exact stage operator: random errors (left), the same T = 0.54 error at every stage (right).

What to say: A systematic error accumulates: F = 0.987 for one gate, 0.913 for eight qubits. Recalibration keeps F = 1. The paper's Eq. 41 (0.50 at N = 8) is a worst case.

Unequal loss between rails Computed · 12_fig5_fig6.py

Shows: Extra loss on the |1⟩ rail of both qubits: F for one gate (left) and for chains (right).

What to say: Equal loss only lowers P. Unequal loss distorts the state: F falls below 0.99 at 1.24 dB of imbalance.

S-bend coupling Computed · 08b_bend_coupling.py

Shows: Three panels: coupling phase gathered along one 15 µm S-bend, κ for straight and curved guides against gap, and the bar-port transmission against gap error with and without the bends.

What to say: The bends give about 30% of the 50:50 phase, so the straight part shrinks from 11.6 to 8.09 µm; the error sensitivities hardly change.

Heater crosstalk Computed · 09_thermal_crosstalk.pyAssumed geometry · stack

Shows: Three panels from the earlier 3D heat model: temperature in the core layer around one heater, crosstalk against rail separation, and the design knobs (stack, pitch, trenches, die thickness).

What to say: Crosstalk travels through the silicon substrate, so it is long-range but small, and oxide trenches do not help. On the exact layout it reaches about 2% (Chip layout tab), and recalibrating the nine drives together removes it.

Electro-optic phase shifters in silicon Computed · 13_phase_shifter_study.py

Shows: Carrier-depletion phase and loss against bias, carrier-injection loss against phase, and the depletion doping trade-off.

What to say: Fast silicon shifters pay in optical loss: about 5 dB for a full 2π depletion shifter, and injection loss that grows with the phase.

Phase shifters inside the gate Computed · 13_phase_shifter_study.pyLiterature values · thin-film LN

Shows: F and P of the gate when each phase is set by a heater, by silicon depletion or injection, by a heater plus a short EO trim, or by thin-film LN.

What to say: Heaters keep F = 1 and P = 1/9. Full-range silicon EO loses most of the photons. Heaters plus a short EO section is the practical design.

Temperature field of one heater Computed · audit re-implementationAssumed geometry · stack

Shows: Temperature rise around one heater from the independent re-implementation.

What to say: Heat spreads into the substrate and reaches the other MZIs, which is why trenches in the oxide do not help.

Heater-to-phase matrix Computed · audit re-implementation

Shows: The full 9 × 9 crosstalk matrix.

What to say: The diagonal is about 160 rad/W; every off-diagonal term is below 1% of it.

Chip layout: reference design, to scale

In plain words: This is the chip drawn exactly as it would be sent for fabrication, from the same numbers the simulations use: the three MZIs, every coupler with its bends, the nine heaters with two wires each, 18 bond pads and a row of test structures. The same drawing exists as a GDS file that opens in KLayout, and the views below are the geometries a COMSOL model would be built on.

Where the numbers come from. Computed values come from this project's scripts (coupler from the mode solver and bend model). Assumed geometry values are typical choices kept identical to the 3D thermal model (rail pitch, heater lengths, layer stack) or standard foundry values (pads, tapers, fibre pitch); a foundry design kit would replace them. Nothing here has been fabricated.

Whole die, top view To scale Computed · 14_reference_layout.py

Light enters on the left (m0 to m5) and leaves on the right. Each MZI: φ heaters (staggered so every heater can be wired), first coupler, θ heater on the upper arm, second coupler. Pads on the top edge drive MZIs A and B; pads on the bottom edge drive MZI C ("+" and "−" are the two ends of each heater). Dashed red lines A and B mark the cross-sections shown below. Design-rule check in the script: 0 wire overlaps, 0 wires over another heater.

One coupler region, MZI A To scale Computed · bend model + layout

The two arms come in from 52 µm apart through a 60 µm routing bend, then the 15 µm coupler bend sets the final approach. About 30% of the 50:50 coupling happens in these coupler bends, which is why the straight part is only 8.09 µm instead of 11.6 µm (Bends & thermal tab). In COMSOL this is the 3D (or 2.5D) propagation model.

Coupler gap at nanometre scale To scale

Cross-section A–A, through the coupler To scale Assumed geometry · stack

The geometry of the 2D mode analysis on the EM tab: two 450 × 220 nm cores, 200 nm apart, on 2 µm of buried oxide. This is COMSOL model 1.

Cross-section B–B, through a θ heater To scale Assumed geometry · stack

The geometry of the heat-transfer model: TiN heater 1 µm above the core. The light is 1.5 × 10⁻⁷ of its peak there, so the metal adds no loss. This is COMSOL model 2 (heat transfer coupled to the optics).

Same solver and grid density, now with this layout's heater positions, 158 µm coupler regions and 1.4 × 1.86 mm die (140,672 unknowns). Crosstalk is higher on the real layout because the heater sections are longer and staggered (needed for wiring), so each rail collects more of the heat from its neighbours; it is still about 2% at most, and recalibrating the nine drives together restores F = 1. Files

  • Download the GDS file (1 nm grid). Layers: 1 Si waveguide, 11 TiN heater, 12 heater contact, 13 metal wire, 14 bond pad, 20 MMI, 30 grating coupler, 99 die outline, 100 labels. Open with KLayout (free).
  • 14_reference_layout.py writes the GDS and layout_geometry.json; 15_thermal_on_layout.py re-runs the thermal model on it.
  • For COMSOL: model 1 = cross-section A–A (mode analysis), model 2 = cross-section B–B (heat transfer + thermo-optic), model 3 = the coupler region above (3D propagation).

What to measure on the first chip

  • The five coupler test cells (gap 160 to 240 nm) give measured splitting against gap, which replaces the simulated ε per nm.
  • The MMI cell gives the directional-coupler versus MMI comparison.
  • Sweeping each heater gives Pπ and the crosstalk matrix, compared with the thermal model above.
  • Classical light through the whole gate gives the 6 × 6 transfer matrix; F and P then follow from the same permanent formula as the simulator.

EM model: coupler cross-section, supermodes and 50:50 length

In plain words: How much light jumps between two neighbouring waveguides depends on the gap between them. This tab solves the light’s field shapes (the even and odd supermodes), and from them the coupling strength κ, the length that gives a 50:50 split, and how κ shifts with gap, width and wavelength.

This is the model that COMSOL would hold: two coupled strip waveguides, a mode analysis at 1550 nm, and a parametric sweep over gap. The solver here reports the even and odd supermodes; their index difference sets the coupling and therefore the length that gives a 50:50 split.

Independent check against a full-vector solver (femwell) Computed · femwell, first audit only

Quantity (450×220 nm, 200 nm gap, 1550 nm)This solverfemwellDifference
Coupling strength κ00.0676 /µm0.0650 /µmthis solver about 4% high

d ln κ / d gap−8.57 /µm−8.49 /µmagree within 1%

Absolute neff, single 450×220 nm guide2.4082.353this solver about 2.3% high

femwell reproduces the textbook neff ≈ 2.445 for a 500×220 nm wire and its κ0 moves by only 0.2% between 1,268 and 5,257 mesh nodes. What this means: the gap-to-ε mapping that the fidelity story rests on holds (6 nm of gap error gives ε ≈ +0.04). The width-to-ε mapping is probably about 15–18% too weak, so yields that include width error are slightly optimistic. Femwell is not COMSOL: this is supporting evidence, and COMSOL validation is still planned. Values were obtained by an earlier audit run of 11_femwell_cross_check.py.

Where this solver is weaker than a full 3D vector solver

  • Semi-vectorial approximation: absolute neff is about 2% high (0.04 to 0.08) against a full-vector solver, and the width sensitivity of κ is about 18% too weak. The gap sensitivity, which matters most for the fidelity result, agrees within 1%.
  • The solver above handles the straight section. The S-bends are estimated separately on the Bends & thermal tab: they supply about 30% of the coupling phase and shorten the straight part to about 8.1 µm, but leave the error sensitivities almost unchanged. Bend radiation loss is not modelled. A 3D mode-expansion or FDTD run settles the rest.
  • Dispersion uses standard Si and SiO₂ index models. Sidewall angle, roughness and cladding stress are not included.

From fabrication tolerance to gate fidelity

In plain words: Nanometre errors become gate fidelity here. Each cell of the grid is a batch of simulated random chips. The strategy buttons show what the heaters can recover: nothing, the paper’s three-phase retuning, or all six phases.

The EM sensitivities turn nanometre-scale fabrication errors into the coupler error ε that the gate model already uses (T = 0.5 + ε). Each cell is 60 random chips run through the exact six-mode model from gate_core.py.

Mean conditional fidelity F Computed · step2b_fab.py

Rows: common gap error shared by all six couplers (1σ, nm). Columns: independent gap and width error on each coupler (1σ, nm). Select a cell. Each cell is 60 random chips, so neighbouring cells differ by about ±0.003 from sampling alone.

S-bend coupling and 3D thermal crosstalk

In plain words: Two refinements. The curved sections that bring the waveguides together also couple a little, so the straight part can be shorter. And a hot heater warms its neighbours through the silicon, so changing one heater slightly moves the others. Both use an assumed layout.

Two models added after the coupler solver: the coupling collected in the S-bends, and heater-to-waveguide heat flow from a 3D conduction model. Both replace earlier assumptions. They are pre-COMSOL estimates.

Read this first. The thermal geometry (heater lengths, 52 µm rail pitch, block positions, layer thicknesses) is assumed, not taken from a foundry kit. Curvature is handled by a conformal-map equivalent index in the 2D semi-vectorial solver, with no bend radiation loss. Re-run the scripts in the delivered folder before quoting numbers.

S-bend coupling

The coupling phase is integrated along the whole coupler, κ(gap(s), curvature(s)) ds, with 50:50 at a total phase of π/4. With 15 µm cosine S-bends and a 1.5 µm offset, the bends supply about 30% of that phase, so the straight part needs only about 8.1 µm instead of 11.6 µm. The sensitivities barely move, so the conclusions on the Fabrication tab stand.

Heater crosstalk from a 3D heat model

Finite-volume oxide stack on a graded grid, the silicon substrate solved exactly by a Fourier map, 1.96×10⁻⁴ per K thermo-optic coefficient from the mode solver. About 19 mW per π on a φ heater. Nearest neighbours leak about 0.8% and other blocks at most 0.3%, far below the 1% to 5% in the assumed-decay chart on the Additions tab.

Inverting the 9×9 matrix alone does not help, because heat also lands on three phases per MZI that have no heater of their own. Recalibrating all nine drives against fidelity recovers F.

Phase shifters: thermo-optic versus electro-optic

In plain words: Every phase in the gate is set by a phase shifter. A heater (thermo-optic) warms the waveguide: it adds no loss but is slow and uses power. An electrical shifter (electro-optic) moves charge carriers or uses a crystal effect: it is fast, but in silicon the carriers also absorb light. For a quantum gate, lost light means lost photons, so loss matters as much as speed.

Each of the nine drive phases is set by one shifter of the chosen type. Its loss, which can depend on the phase it gives, goes into the exact six-mode model. F and P are shown with the nominal drives and after re-tuning all nine drives. Run 13_phase_shifter_study.py to reproduce.

Read this first. Silicon depletion and injection use the Soref–Bennett free-carrier model on this project's own mode, with the doping in the 450 × 220 nm core only (no slab, contacts or series resistance). This gives VπL about 1.0 V·cm at 5×10¹⁷ cm⁻³, better than the 1.4 to 3.1 V·cm measured on real rib devices, so treat EO lengths as optimistic. The heater Pπ comes from the assumed 3D thermal stack. Thin-film LN numbers are from the literature. Pre-COMSOL estimates.

When every shifter loses the same amount ("balanced"), the loss is the same on every photon path: F stays at 1 and only P falls, exactly as the paper's Eq. 42 predicts (0.25 dB per shifter is 0.5 dB per photon, so P = 0.0882). When the loss differs between arms, or changes with the phase, the gate itself is distorted and F drops.

Silicon depletion, 5×10¹⁷ cm⁻³ Computed · Soref–Bennett

More reverse bias widens the depleted region (from 69 nm to 189 nm), which raises the index and lowers the loss. A full 2π needs 4.8 mm and costs about 5.3 dB, all from the doping.

Silicon injection, 500 µm Computed · Soref–Bennett

Injected carriers shift the phase strongly but absorb in proportion: about 1.5 dB for π. Because loss follows the phase, shifters set to different phases lose different amounts, which unbalances the interference.

Depletion trade-off against doping Computed

Heavier doping shortens the shifter (lower VπL) but raises the loss faster, so a full-range depletion shifter costs 2.3 to 8.4 dB whatever doping is chosen.

What this means for the design

  • Static gate phases: heaters. They add no measurable loss: the mode's intensity 1 µm above the core is only about 1.5 × 10⁻⁷ of its peak, so the TiN never sees the light. The cost is about 175 mW for the nine heaters and µs-scale settling.
  • Fast corrections: a short EO section next to the heater. A 228 µm depletion trim with 0.3 rad of range costs 0.25 dB. If both arms carry one, F stays at 1 and P drops to 79% of ideal.
  • Full-range silicon EO is a poor fit for a post-selected gate: P falls to a few percent of ideal.
  • Low-loss Pockels materials (thin-film LN, BTO) avoid the carrier loss and are the route to fast, feed-forward cascades, at the cost of a hybrid platform.
  • Heater crosstalk, its 3D model and recalibration are on the Bends & thermal tab; DAC resolution in script 05.
